title: The Ethics of Machine Judgement
text:
Automated systems now help decide who receives a loan, a job interview or a medical referral. Their supporters argue that algorithms are more consistent than human officials, yet this consistency can conceal the prejudices embedded in the historical data used to train them. Consequently, a decision that appears neutral may simply reproduce past inequalities at a far greater scale.

Accountability is therefore the central difficulty. When a person is rejected by a model, it is often unclear who is responsible: the engineers who built it, the organisation that deployed it or the data that shaped its behaviour. Many scholars contend that meaningful transparency, including the right to challenge an outcome, should be treated as a condition of legitimate use rather than an optional courtesy.

questions.text: According to paragraph one, what do supporters of automated systems claim?
options: Algorithms are more consistent than human officials
Automated systems are cheaper to build than manual ones
Medical referrals should be decided by machines alone

questions.text: According to paragraph two, what do many scholars consider meaningful transparency to include?
options: The right to challenge an outcome
Publishing the source code of every company
Removing all human officials from decisions
Limiting automated systems to loans only

questions.text: What can be inferred about a decision that appears neutral but was trained on biased historical data?
options: It may quietly repeat earlier unfairness on a larger scale
It is guaranteed to be fairer than any human decision
It can only be used for medical referrals
It has no connection to the people it affects

questions.text: Which conclusion best follows from the passage as a whole?
options: Legitimate use of automated systems depends on accountability and the possibility of challenge
Automated systems should replace all human judgement immediately
Responsibility for rejections is always clearly assigned
Consistency alone is sufficient to justify a model's decisions

paragraph_translations: Zautomatyzowane systemy pomagają obecnie decydować, kto otrzyma kredyt, rozmowę kwalifikacyjną lub skierowanie na badania. Ich zwolennicy twierdzą, że algorytmy są bardziej spójne niż urzędnicy, jednak ta spójność może ukrywać uprzedzenia zakorzenione w danych historycznych, na których je trenowano. W rezultacie decyzja pozornie neutralna może po prostu odtwarzać dawne nierówności na znacznie większą skalę.

Odpowiedzialność jest więc główną trudnością. Gdy model odrzuca daną osobę, często nie wiadomo, kto ponosi odpowiedzialność: inżynierowie, którzy go zbudowali, organizacja, która go wdrożyła, czy dane, które ukształtowały jego działanie. Wielu badaczy twierdzi, że istotna przejrzystość, w tym prawo do zakwestionowania wyniku, powinna być warunkiem uprawnionego użycia, a nie opcjonalną uprzejmością.
